findings.title: Role-mapping checks drop the manage-clients admin role
findings.body: canMapRoles, canMapCompositeRoles, and canMapClientScopeRoles only call hasPermission. Unlike canManage(ClientModel) and canView(), they never call root.hasOneAdminRole(AdminRoles.MANAGE_CLIENTS) and they do not delegate to the parent implementation that treated that role as a short-circuit. AdminPermissions.evaluator installs this class for every realm whenever ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled, including realms that have not turned on fine-grained admin permissions. A master admin or a realm admin who only has the manage-clients role therefore gets false from these methods (hasPermission also returns false when the admin is from another realm). Client role assignment and composite/client-scope role mapping that previously succeeded are denied. The new interface javadoc documents the same omission, so callers cannot rely on it either.

findings.title: A per-client resource hides all-clients policies
findings.body: hasPermission(ClientModel, scope) evaluates only the resource named with that client's id when one exists. The all-clients resource is consulted only when findByName returns null. Any object permission (for example VIEW on one client) therefore suppresses all-clients grants for every other scope. canManage(client), canConfigure, canMapRoles, canMapCompositeRoles, and canMapClientScopeRoles all go through this helper, and only canView() checks the all-clients resource independently. A policy that manages or maps roles for all clients will not apply to a client that already has any dedicated resource, so those operations are incorrectly denied. The reverse is also wrong if a realm-wide negative policy is supposed to deny a scope: once an object resource exists and grants that scope, the all-clients deny is never evaluated. This contradicts the new ClientPermissionEvaluator javadoc, which says all-clients MANAGE, CONFIGURE, VIEW, and MAP_ROLES permissions also grant the corresponding per-client checks.

findings.title: Already-initialized admin-permissions clients never get Clients scopes
findings.body: init still returns immediately when realm.getAdminPermissionsClient() is non-null. That client is created the first time admin permissions are enabled, and earlier versions of this schema only seeded the Users resource type. Realms that already have the client will not get the new configure, map-roles-client-scope, or map-roles-composite scopes, nor the Clients all-resource. Creating a client permission then fails in getScope or in getOrCreateResource ("No scopes found." / scope not found), and evaluation cannot fall back to a Clients resource that was never created. There is no migration in this change to add the missing scopes and resource on startup.

findings.title: Null all-clients resource causes a 500 on permission checks
findings.body: When no per-client resource exists, the code loads the Clients type resource and immediately calls policyStore.findByResource(server, resource) without a null check. getResourceTypeResource returns null when admin-permissions schema support is off, when the type is unknown, or when the Clients resource was never created (the upgrade case above). The usual PolicyStore implementation dereferences resource.getId(), so the admin API throws NullPointerException instead of denying the call. The sibling hasPermission(String) path does null-check findByName and returns false; this path should do the same.

findings.title: Existing client permission methods now throw UnsupportedOperationException
findings.body: canExchangeTo, isPermissionsEnabled, setPermissionsEnabled, getPermissions, resource, and the Policy accessors are overridden to throw UnsupportedOperationException. MgmtPermissionsV2 is selected solely because ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled, so these overrides replace working boolean/Policy behavior for every realm. Token exchange calls canExchangeTo (and often isPermissionsEnabled first); the admin client permissions endpoints call getPermissions and setPermissionsEnabled. Those callers expect false, an empty map, or a 403, not an unchecked exception, so enabling the feature turns token exchange and the client permissions admin API into HTTP 500s even when the realm is not using Clients permissions. Returning a deny/no-op, as the V1 methods did when permissions were not enabled, is required until V2 implements them.

findings.title: Removal cleanup is gated on the wrong feature flag
findings.body: The client/role/group removal listener now runs only when ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1) is enabled. The evaluator switches to MgmtPermissionsV2 whenever ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled, regardless of the V1 flag. With neither flag on (the default), deletion no longer calls setPermissionsEnabled(false), so fine-grained permission data created while V1 was previously enabled is left behind and can break client deletion with leftover authorization rows. With both flags on, management() returns V2 and setPermissionsEnabled throws UnsupportedOperationException, which fails the removal transaction. The guard needs to follow the same V2 switch as AdminPermissions.evaluator: skip or replace the V1 cleanup only when V2 is the active implementation.

findings.title: Client resources are displayed as a null name
findings.body: getResourceName resolves Users resources to the username, but the new Clients branch is missing. Per-client resources are stored with name equal to the internal client id (resolveClient) and getOrCreateResource never sets a display name, so the method returns resource.getDisplayName(), which is null. Permission list/detail APIs and the admin UI therefore show a blank resource for every client-specific permission instead of the clientId. A deleted client is also not reported, whereas a missing user throws ModelIllegalStateException.

findings.title: requireView javadoc describes a boolean return
findings.body: requireView and requireViewClientScopes are void and throw ForbiddenException when the matching can* method is false, which is what the other require* javadocs in this interface say. These two comments instead say "Returns true if canView()/canViewClientScopes() returns true", which is the contract of the boolean methods above them. Callers reading only the new javadoc will not know that the methods throw.
